title: Tools for Research Data Management and curation
text:
This book collects well-documented R functions and hands-on workflows to support research data management (RDM) in practice — from ingest and validation to metadata enrichment, curation, and reporting.


How to read this book: Each chapter introduces a task area (e.g., ingest, quality control). For each function, you’ll find its purpose, arguments, return value, examples, tests, and references. Copy/paste-ready snippets are provided in callouts.







Tip



Reproducibility first. All examples rely on versioned functions in R/ with deterministic behavior and unit tests where applicable.

title: 5  Guide to opening and inspecting GeoPackage (.gpkg) files
text:
5.1 Overview
A GeoPackage (.gpkg) is an open, standards-based file format for geospatial information. It as a versatile that can hold multiple layers of vector features (points, lines, polygons), raster imagery, and even non-spatial tables. Its self-contained nature makes it an excellent format for data distribution and archival.
This document provides a guide for curators and researchers on how to programmatically inspect, read, and visualize the contents of a .gpkg file using R. It also suggests powerful external tools for deeper visual exploration.

5.5 Visualize the Data
We can create both static and interactive maps for geospacial data.

5.5.1 Static Plot
For a quick, simple preview of the geometry, the base plot() function works well.


Code
# [cite_start]Create a static plot of the layer's geometry [cite: 1]
plot(st_geometry(gpkg_data))









Code
# You can also color the plot based on a specific data column
# plot(gpkg_data["ATTRIBUTE_NAME"])




5.5.2 Interactive Map
For more compelling exploration, the leaflet package can create an interactive map that you can pan and zoom.First, the coordinates nned to be transformed to EPSG:4326 to be read by leaflet.
The leaflet package has different functions for each geometry type:

addPolygons() for areas.
addPolylines() for lines.
addCircleMarkers() or addMarkers() for points.



Code
# 1. Transform the data to the CRS that Leaflet expects (EPSG:4326)
gpkg_data_wgs84 <- st_transform(gpkg_data, crs = 4326)

# 2. Now, create the map using the *transformed* data
leaflet(gpkg_data_wgs84) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addCircleMarkers(
    radius = 3,         # Sets the circle size in pixels
    stroke = FALSE,     # Removes the circle outline
    fillOpacity = 0.8,  # Sets the transparency of the circle
    popup = ~paste0("<strong>Attribute: </strong>", as.character(gpkg_data_wgs84[[1]]))
  )




Interactive map of the data, correctly projected in WGS 84 for web display.

title: 2  Automated CSV File Checker
text:
Discover files: Automatically find all .csv files in the project directory.
Extract metadata: For each file, gather information on column names, data types, and row counts.
Calculate descriptive statistics: Compute summary statistics (min, max, mean, median) and the count of missing values (NA) for each column.
Generate summary outputs: Create two final .csv files:

MetaData_CSV.csv: A detailed, long-format summary of every column from every file.
ColumnCheck_CSV.csv: A wide-format summary to easily compare column names and types across all files.




This notebook is located and run in the root directory of the data deposit.
All compressed files (e.g., .zip, .tar) have already been extracted.

text:
2.4 Generate metadata summaries
Here, the code will loop through each full file path in our csv.files list, read the file, and extract the required metadata.

2.4.1 Initializing the summary table

csv.summ <- data.frame(
  file.name = character(),
  column.name = character(),
  column.type = character(),
  rows = integer(),
  min = character(),
  mean = character(),
  med = character(),
  max = character(),
  NAs = character()
)



2.4.2 Processing each file
Here, we systematically loops through each CSV file selected to summarize the data and handle errors. For valid data, we extract metadata (like column names, data types, and row count), and calculate descriptive statistics (min, mean, max, and a count of missing values). When not valid columns are found (corrupted or contains unexpected data types) the script print a detailed message in the console identifying the problematic file and the specific error.

# The Main Loop: Processing Each File
for (i in csv.files) {
  
  # Use tryCatch to handle potential errors in a file without stopping the whole script

2.10 Extract extensions and generate summary table
The code takes the complete list of file paths and performs two steps:

Extract extensions: It isolates the file extension from each path. The logic is designed to handle files with multiple dots (e.g., archive.tar.gz) and files with no extension at all.
Count and summarize: It then counts the occurrences of each unique extension and sorts the results to show the most common file types first.

#| label: generate-summary

file_summary <- tibble(FilePath = all_files) %>%
  mutate(
    # basename() gets just the filename from the full path
    FileName = basename(FilePath),
    # Use stringr for a more readable and robust extraction
    Extension = str_extract(FileName, "(?<=\\.)[^.]+$") %>%
      # If no extension is found (returns NA), replace with a descriptor
      replace_na("(no extension)")
  ) %>%
  count(Extension, name = "Count", sort = TRUE)

8.1 Overview
A GeoPackage (.gpkg) is an open, standards-based file format for geospatial information. It as a versatile that can hold multiple layers of vector features (points, lines, polygons), raster imagery, and even non-spatial tables. This document provides a guide for curators and researchers on how to programmatically inspect, read, and visualize the contents of a .gpkg file using R. It also suggests powerful external tools for deeper visual exploration.

9.1 Overview
This tool provides an automated workflow for extracting and summarizing metadata from a collection of NetCDF (.nc) file, a self-describing format common in scientific fields. The workflow performs three main tasks:

title: 9  NetCDF Files
text:
File discovery: It scans a specified directory for all NetCDF files.
Metadata extraction: It uses the tidync package to pull out three fundamental components from each file:

Dimensions: The axes of the data grid (e.g., latitude, longitude, time).
Variables: The actual data stored in the file (e.g., temperature, pressure).
Attributes: Descriptive metadata, which can be global (applying to the whole file) or attached to specific variables (e.g., units).

Report generation: It reshapes this metadata into user-friendly summary tables and saves them as .csv files.

9.5 Extract and organize metadata
Here, we will process each NetCDF file using purrr::map functions to extract its dimensions, variables, and attributes.


Code
# Create a "safely" version of tidync to handle potentially corrupt files
safe_tidync <- purrr::safely(tidync)

# 1. Process all files, safely handling any errors
processed_files <- purrr::map(nc_files, ~safe_tidync(.x)) %>% 
  set_names(nc_files)

# 2. Separate successful results from errors
successful_results <- purrr::map(processed_files, "result") %>% 
  purrr::compact()

errors <- purrr::map(processed_files, "error") %>% 
  purrr::compact()

# Report any files that failed to process
if (length(errors) > 0) {
  message("The following files failed to process and were skipped:")
  walk(names(errors), message)
}

# 3. Extract and combine dimensions, variables, and attributes
nc_dimensions <- purrr::map(successful_results, ~.x$dimension) %>% 
  bind_rows(.id = "FileName")

nc_variables <- purrr::map(successful_results, ~.x$variable) %>% 
  bind_rows(.id = "FileName")

nc_attributes <- purrr::map(successful_results, ~.x$attribute) %>% 
  bind_rows(.id = "FileName")

print("Metadata extraction complete.")

# 1. Initialize an empty list to store results
all_sheets_summary <- list()

# 2. Loop over each Excel file
for (file_path in excel_files) {
  
  file_name <- basename(file_path)
  
  # Use a tryCatch in case the file is corrupt or password-protected
  tryCatch({
    
    # Check 1: List all sheet names
    sheet_names <- excel_sheets(file_path)
    
    if (length(sheet_names) == 0) {
      # Handle empty workbooks
      all_sheets_summary[[length(all_sheets_summary) + 1]] <- tibble(
        FileName = file_name,
        SheetName = "(No Sheets Found)",
        Dimensions = "0 x 0",
        IsLikelyNonTabular = TRUE,
        HeaderPreview = "(Empty)"
      )
      next # Skip to the next file
    }
    
    # 3. Loop over each sheet in the workbook
    for (sheet_name in sheet_names) {
      
      # Use a tryCatch for each sheet (a sheet might be corrupt)
      tryCatch({
        
        # Check 2: Get true dimensions by reading the whole sheet
        # We specify .name_repair to prevent messages
        full_sheet_data <- read_excel(file_path, sheet = sheet_name, .name_repair = "minimal")
        true_dims <- paste(dim(full_sheet_data), collapse = " x ")
        
        # Check 3 & 4: Read headers and check for non-tabular data
        # We use .name_repair = "minimal" to detect default '...#' names
        header_preview <- read_excel(file_path, sheet = sheet_name, n_max = 5, .name_repair = "minimal")
        col_names <- colnames(header_preview)
        
        # This is a proxy. It's TRUE if:
        # a) Any column name is a default '...#' (often means merged headers)
        # b) There is only 1 column (often means a chart or text block)
        is_non_tabular <- any(str_detect(col_names, "^\\.\\.\\.\\d+$")) || length(col_names) <= 1
        
        # Store the first 5 rows' headers as a single string
        header_as_string <- paste(col_names, collapse = " | ")
        
        # Add results to our list
        all_sheets_summary[[length(all_sheets_summary) + 1]] <- tibble(
          FileName = file_name,
          SheetName = sheet_name,
          Dimensions = true_dims,
          IsLikelyNonTabular = is_non_tabular,
          HeaderPreview = header_as_string
        )
        
      }, error = function(e_sheet) {
        # Handle a single bad sheet
        message(paste("Error on sheet:", sheet_name, "in file:", file_name, "|", e_sheet$message))
        all_sheets_summary[[length(all_sheets_summary) + 1]] <- tibble(
          FileName = file_name,
          SheetName = sheet_name,
          Dimensions = "Error",
          IsLikelyNonTabular = TRUE,
          HeaderPreview = paste("ERROR:", e_sheet$message)
        )
      })
    }
    
  }, error = function(e_file) {
    # Handle a single bad file
    message(paste("Error on file:", file_name, "|", e_file$message))
    all_sheets_summary[[length(all_sheets_summary) + 1]] <- tibble(
      FileName = file_name,
      SheetName = "Error",
      Dimensions = "Error",
      IsLikelyNonTabular = TRUE,
      HeaderPreview = paste("ERROR:", e_file$message)

# FUNCTION: Checks the file's first 4 bytes for the HDF5 signature
# This is a robust way to identify MATLAB v7.3 files.
is_v73_hdf5 <- function(path) {
  # Open file in binary read mode
  con <- file(path, "rb")
  # Ensure connection is closed when the function exits
  on.exit(close(con)) 
  
  # Read the first 4 bytes (HDF5 signature starts with 0x89HDF)
  header <- tryCatch({
    readBin(con, what = "raw", n = 4, size = 1)
  }, error = function(e) {
    # File might be too small or inaccessible
    return(as.raw(0))
  })
  
  # Check if the header matches the HDF5 signature
  return(identical(header, as.raw(c(0x89, 0x48, 0x44, 0x46))))
}

7.4 Generate Metadata Report
MATLAB files come in two broad categories:

v4/v5 files, stored in a proprietary binary format
v7.3 files, stored as HDF5 (Hierarchical Data Format)

We try to read each .mat file as HDF5 first. If that succeeds, we extract:

variable (dataset) names
data type (HDF5 class)
array dimensions
number of dimensions

If the file is not HDF5, the code falls back to R.matlab::readMat() and extracts the same information from a v4/v5 structure.

if (length(mat_files) == 0) {

# Helper to parse dims from either numeric vector or "3000 x 180 x 180" string
parse_dims <- function(d) {
  # Missing
  if (is.null(d) || (length(d) == 1 && is.na(d))) {
    return(list(str = "-", n_dim = 0L, n_el = NA_integer_))
  }

  # Character like "3000 x 180 x 180"
  if (is.character(d)) {
    parts <- strsplit(d, "x|×")[[1]]
    parts <- trimws(parts)
    parts <- parts[parts != ""]
    nums  <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(parts))

    if (length(nums) == 0 || all(is.na(nums))) {
      # Fallback: just show raw string
      return(list(str = d, n_dim = NA_integer_, n_el = NA_integer_))
    } else {
      return(list(
        str   = paste(nums, collapse = " x "),
        n_dim = length(nums),
        n_el  = as.integer(prod(nums))
      ))
    }
  }

  # Numeric or integer vector
  nums <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(d))
  nums <- nums[!is.na(nums)]
  if (length(nums) == 0) {
    return(list(str = "-", n_dim = 0L, n_el = NA_integer_))
  } else {
    return(list(
      str   = paste(nums, collapse = " x "),
      n_dim = length(nums),
      n_el  = as.integer(prod(nums))
    ))
  }
}

file_summary_list <- list()
var_summary_list  <- list()
idx <- 1L

for (file_path in mat_files) {
  file_name <- basename(file_path)
  cat("\n--- Processing file:", file_name, "---\n")

  file_size_mb <- round(file.info(file_path)$size / (1024^2), 3)

  # 1) TRY: read as HDF5 (MAT v7.3)
  res <- tryCatch({
    f <- hdf5r::H5File$new(file_path, mode = "r")

    # Make sure closing the file never throws a hard error
    on.exit(
      tryCatch(
        f$close_all(),
        error = function(e) {
          message("  close_all() warning for ", file_name, ": ", e$message)
        }
      ),
      add = TRUE
    )

    listing <- f$ls(recursive = TRUE)

    # Keep only datasets
    ds <- listing[listing$obj_type == "H5I_DATASET", , drop = FALSE]

    if (nrow(ds) == 0) stop("HDF5 file contains no datasets")

    dims_list <- ds$dataset.dims

    parsed <- lapply(dims_list, parse_dims)

    dims_str  <- vapply(parsed, function(x) x$str,   character(1))
    num_dims  <- vapply(parsed, function(x) x$n_dim, integer(1))
    num_elems <- vapply(parsed, function(x) x$n_el,  integer(1))

    out <- tibble::tibble(
      FileName      = file_name,
      VariableName  = ds$name,
      Class         = as.character(ds$dataset.type_class),
      Dimensions    = dims_str,
      NumDimensions = num_dims,
      NumElements   = num_elems,
      Format        = "v7.3 (HDF5)"
    )

    cat("  Read as HDF5 (v7.3);", nrow(out), "datasets.\n")
    out
  },
  error = function(e) {
    cat("  HDF5 attempt failed for ", file_name, ": ",
        conditionMessage(e), "\n", sep = "")
    NULL
  })

  # 2) FALLBACK: classic MAT (v4/v5) via readMat, only if HDF5 failed
  if (is.null(res)) {
    res <- tryCatch({
      mat_data  <- R.matlab::readMat(file_path)
      var_names <- names(mat_data)

      if (length(var_names) == 0) {
        cat("  readMat(): file appears empty.\n")
        tibble::tibble(
          FileName      = file_name,
          VariableName  = "(Empty)",
          Class         = "-",
          Dimensions    = "-",
          NumDimensions = 0L,
          NumElements   = NA_integer_,
          Format        = "v4/v5"
        )
      } else {
        cat("  readMat(): ", length(var_names), " variables.\n", sep = "")
        purrr::map_dfr(var_names, function(var) {
          obj  <- mat_data[[var]]
          dims <- dim(obj)
          dims_str <- if (is.null(dims)) {
            paste(length(obj), "(len)")
          } else {
            paste(as.integer(dims), collapse = " x ")
          }
          n_dim <- if (is.null(dims)) 1L else length(dims)
          n_el  <- if (is.null(dims)) length(obj) else as.integer(prod(dims))

          tibble::tibble(
            FileName      = file_name,
            VariableName  = var,
            Class         = class(obj)[1],
            Dimensions    = dims_str,
            NumDimensions = n_dim,
            NumElements   = n_el,
            Format        = "v4/v5"
          )
        })
      }
    },
    error = function(e) {
      cat("  readMat() failed for ", file_name, ": ",
          conditionMessage(e), "\n", sep = "")
      tibble::tibble(
        FileName      = file_name,
        VariableName  = "ERROR",
        Class         = "Error",
        Dimensions    = paste("Failed to read:", conditionMessage(e)),
        NumDimensions = NA_integer_,
        NumElements   = NA_integer_,
        Format        = "Unknown"
      )
    })
  }

  # File-level summary
  file_summary_list[[idx]] <- tibble::tibble(
    FileName     = file_name,
    FullPath     = normalizePath(file_path),
    Format       = unique(res$Format)[1],
    FileSize_MB  = file_size_mb,
    NumVariables = nrow(res)
  )

  # Variable-level summary
  var_summary_list[[idx]] <- res
  idx <- idx + 1L
}

title: 6  SPSS (.sav) Files
text:
6.5 Generate Data Dictionary
Here, the code loops through every file found and performs the following:

Reads the Header: It reads only the first 100 rows (n_max = 100). This makes the process extremely fast, even for multi-gigabyte files, because we only need the metadata headers, not the full dataset.
Extracts Metadata: It uses the attr() function to pull out the hidden “label” and “labels” attributes attached to each column.
Formats Output: It creates a tidy table listing every variable, its type, and its definitions.



Code
message("Generating Data Dictionary...")

# Map over every file found
report <- purrr::map_dfr(spss_files, function(file_path) {
  
  fname <- basename(file_path)
  
  tryCatch({
    # Read a small subset to get metadata without memory overhead
    data <- read_sav(file_path, n_max = 100)
    
    # Map over every column (variable) in the dataset
    purrr::map_dfr(names(data), function(var) {
      
      # Extract the column object
      col <- data[[var]]
      
      # 1. Get Variable Label (The "Question")
      lbl <- attr(col, "label", exact = TRUE)
      if (is.null(lbl)) lbl <- "(No Label)"
      
      # 2. Get Value Labels (The "Answers")
      # These come as a named vector: c(Yes = 1, No = 0)
      val_lbls <- attr(col, "labels", exact = TRUE)
      
      # Format value labels into a readable string: "1=Yes; 0=No"
      if (!is.null(val_lbls)) {
        val_str <- paste(val_lbls, names(val_lbls), sep="=", collapse="; ")
      } else {
        val_str <- ""
      }
      
      # 3. Create Summary Row
      tibble(
        FileName = fname,
        TotalRowsInFile = nrow(data), # Note: If n_max used, this is partial
        VariableName = var,
        VariableLabel = lbl,
        DataType = class(col)[1], # e.g., haven_labelled, numeric, character
        ValueLabels = substr(val_str, 1, 100) # Truncate long lists for readability
      )
    })
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    # Error Handling: If file is corrupt
    tibble(
      FileName = fname, 
      VariableName = "ERROR", 
      VariableLabel = e$message, 
      DataType = "Error", 
      ValueLabels = ""
    )
  })
})

text:
7.7 Curation Insights
Use the output CSV to check for these common issues:

Truncated Labels: Older versions of Stata (v12 and earlier) had strict character limits (80 characters) for variable labels. Check if descriptions are cut off mid-sentence.
Date/Time Formatting: Stata handles dates differently than R. Check the DataType column. If you see raw numbers (e.g., 14832) where you expect dates, confirm that the file format version is compatible or note that conversion will be required.
Missing Descriptions: Filter for VariableLabel == “(No Label)”. In Stata datasets, abbreviated variable names (e.g., x1, y_cnt) are common; without labels, these variables are functionally useless to secondary users.
